title: P5 Social Studies — Term Three, Week One, Lesson One: Arms of Government

blocks.text: Government is the group of people and institutions that make public decisions and provide services for a country. In Uganda there are national and local governments.

By the end of this lesson, the learner should be able to:
• Define government.
• Name the three arms of government.
• Explain the main work of each arm.
Learners know that villages have leaders and that schools have rules. Ask who helps to lead the village and who makes rules at school.

Government — people and institutions managing public affairs.
Legislature — the arm that makes laws.
Executive — the arm that implements laws.
Judiciary — the arm that interprets laws and settles disputes.
Parliament — the national law-making institution.
Meaning of government
Government is the group of people and institutions responsible for managing public affairs in a country.

Government helps maintain peace and order.
Government provides services such as schools, health care and roads.
Government protects the rights and safety of people.
Government plans and oversees the use of public resources.
The three arms of government
An arm of government is a major part of government with a special responsibility.
The three arms and their main duties
rows: Makes laws and oversees government work

blocks.text: 1. The Legislature

The Legislature is the law-making arm of government.
Uganda's national legislature is Parliament.
Members of Parliament discuss proposed laws.
Parliament makes and amends laws.
Parliament examines government spending and work.
Parliament represents the concerns of citizens.
2. The Executive

The Executive is responsible for carrying out laws and public policies.
The President is part of the national Executive.
The Cabinet helps direct government policy.
Ministries help manage public services.
The Executive organises the implementation of approved government programmes.
The Executive directs government departments in their work.
3. The Judiciary

The Judiciary interprets and applies laws in court cases.
The courts settle disputes according to the law.
Judges and magistrates make decisions on cases brought before them.
The Judiciary helps protect the rights of people through lawful decisions.
Courts consider evidence and hear the parties in a case.
The Judiciary should decide cases independently and fairly.
Why the arms have different duties

Different arms carry out different responsibilities.
This helps prevent too much power being held in one part of government.
Each arm has duties set out by law.
The arms work within Uganda's Constitution and laws.
Examples from everyday life

When Parliament makes a law, the Legislature is at work.
When a ministry puts a public health programme into action, the Executive is at work.
When a court settles a disagreement, the Judiciary is at work.
Local government is a level of government, not a fourth arm of national government.

If Parliament passes a law, the Legislature is performing its law-making role. If a ministry implements a public programme, the Executive is working. If a court settles a legal dispute, the Judiciary is working.
Divide the class into three groups. Give each group one arm of government to explain using its name, members and main duty.
Match each action to its arm: making laws; carrying out a government programme; settling a court case.

Parliament does not decide court cases: courts exercise judicial power.
The Executive does not replace Parliament when making ordinary laws.
Local government is a level of government; it is not one of the three arms.

Government manages public affairs.
The Legislature makes laws.
The Executive implements laws and programmes.
The Judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes.

1. What is government?
2. Name the three arms of government.
3. Which arm makes laws?
4. Give two duties of Parliament.
5. Which arm implements government programmes?
6. Name two parts of the national Executive.
7. Which arm settles cases brought before courts?
8. State two duties of the Judiciary.
9. Why is it helpful for government to have different arms?
10. Identify the arm at work: (a) Parliament debates a proposed law, (b) a ministry opens a health centre, (c) a court settles a land dispute.
